grammar.title: Talking about habits with nuance
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B2, além de **usually** e **used to**, você tem estruturas que mostram **atitude** sobre o hábito:

**1. Will + verbo (presente)** → hábito **característico** de alguém (muitas vezes com carinho ou resignação):
"My grandma **will** always **offer** you food, even if you've just eaten."
**Would + verbo (passado)** → o mesmo, no passado (só ações, não estados):
"When I was a kid, my dad **would** wake us up singing."

**2. Will / would com ênfase** (WILL, WOULD acentuados) → hábito **irritante**:
"He **WILL** leave his shoes in the middle of the room!" / "She **WOULD** say that — she always takes his side."

**3. Always / constantly / forever + present continuous** → hábito irritante ou surpreendente:
"You're **always losing** your keys!" / "He's **constantly checking** his phone."

**4. Keep (on) + -ing** → repetição (frequentemente irritante): "The printer **keeps jamming**." / "She **kept interrupting** me."

**5. Tend to + verbo** → tendência geral (mais neutro, ótimo para generalizar com cuidado):
"Introverts **tend to** prefer small groups." / "I **tend not to** trust first impressions." (negativa: tend not to / don't tend to)

**6. Be prone to / be inclined to** (mais formal): "He's **prone to** exaggerating."

**Come across as** + adjetivo/substantivo = passar a impressão de ser: "She **comes across as** arrogant, but she's just shy."

rows: She WILL leave the lights on!

examples.en: My boss will reply to emails at 2 a.m. — it's just how he is.
examples.pt: Meu chefe é capaz de responder e-mails às 2 da manhã — é o jeito dele.

examples.en: She tends to come across as cold, but once you get to know her, she's incredibly warm.
examples.pt: Ela costuma passar uma imagem fria, mas quando você a conhece, ela é extremamente calorosa.

examples.en: My roommate is forever leaving dirty dishes in the sink!
examples.pt: Meu colega de casa vive deixando louça suja na pia!

grammar.tip_pt: **Tend to** é uma das palavras mais úteis do B2: ela **suaviza generalizações**. Em vez de "Brazilians are late" (estereótipo), diga "Brazilians **tend to** be more flexible about time".

common_mistakes.wrong: He would be very tall when he was young.
common_mistakes.right: He used to be very tall... / He was very tall...
common_mistakes.why_pt: Would não funciona com estados (be, have, know) — só com ações repetidas.

common_mistakes.wrong: She tends to be talking a lot.
common_mistakes.right: She tends to talk a lot.

common_mistakes.wrong: He seems arrogant, but he comes across as shy.
common_mistakes.right: He comes across as arrogant, but he's actually shy.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Come across as = a impressão (aparente); depois vem a realidade.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Para mostrar irritação, os nativos **acentuam** will/would, que normalmente são fracos: "He **WILL** leave his socks everywhere!" ("rí UÍL lív..."). Compare com o neutro: "He'll sit for hours reading" ("ríl").
practice: He WILL leave his socks everywhere! (irritado)

dialogue.title: The new manager
dialogue.context_pt: Duas colegas comentam suas impressões sobre o novo gerente depois do primeiro mês.

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: So, what do you make of the new manager? He came across as a bit arrogant at first.
lines.pt: E aí, o que você acha do novo gerente? Ele passou uma impressão meio arrogante no começo.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.en: I thought so too, but I think he's just reserved. He tends to think before he speaks, which some people mistake for coldness.
lines.pt: Também achei, mas acho que ele só é reservado. Ele costuma pensar antes de falar, e algumas pessoas confundem isso com frieza.

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: Maybe. Although he does keep interrupting people in meetings.
lines.pt: Talvez. Embora ele fique interrompendo as pessoas nas reuniões.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.en: True, that's annoying. And he will send emails late at night — I got one at 11 p.m. yesterday.
lines.pt: Verdade, isso é irritante. E ele tem mania de mandar e-mails tarde da noite — recebi um às 23h ontem.

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: Our old manager would never do that. She'd always say evenings were sacred.
lines.pt: Nossa antiga gerente nunca faria isso. Ela sempre dizia que as noites eram sagradas.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.en: Well, to be fair, he's quite down-to-earth when you talk to him one-on-one. And he's open-minded — he actually listened to my idea.
lines.pt: Bom, para ser justa, ele é bem pé no chão quando você conversa com ele a sós. E tem a mente aberta — ele realmente ouviu minha ideia.

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: So you're saying we shouldn't judge a book by its cover?
lines.pt: Então você está dizendo que não devemos julgar pelas aparências?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.en: Exactly. Give him another month. First impressions tend to be wrong more often than we think.
lines.pt: Exatamente. Dê mais um mês a ele. Primeiras impressões costumam estar erradas mais vezes do que pensamos.

listening.title: Podcast: the science of first impressions
listening.context_pt: Um psicólogo fala sobre como formamos primeiras impressões.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: Research suggests that we form an impression of someone's face in a fraction of a second — some studies say about a tenth of a second. We tend to judge whether someone is trustworthy, competent or friendly almost instantly. The problem is that these snap judgements are heavily influenced by bias. For example, we tend to see people who look like us as more trustworthy, and we'll often assume that attractive people are also smarter — something psychologists call the halo effect. The good news is that first impressions aren't fixed. If we keep meeting someone and they keep behaving in a way that contradicts our first judgement, we'll eventually update our opinion. The key is to stay curious and to be aware of our own biases.

questions.q: How quickly do we form an impression of a face, according to some studies?
questions.answer: In about a tenth of a second.

questions.q: What is the halo effect?
questions.answer: Assuming that attractive people are also smarter (one positive trait influences others).

questions.q: Whom do we tend to see as more trustworthy?
questions.answer: People who look like us.

questions.q: How can we change a first impression?
questions.answer: By meeting the person repeatedly and staying curious/aware of our biases.

reading.title: Why we misjudge people
reading.text: Imagine meeting two job candidates. One walks in confidently, makes eye contact and tells a funny story. The other speaks quietly and looks down. Most of us would instinctively prefer the first — even though nothing we've seen tells us who would actually do the job better. Psychologists have identified several reasons why our judgements of other people tend to be unreliable. One is the halo effect: when someone has one attractive quality, we'll tend to assume they have others too. Another is the fundamental attribution error: when other people behave badly, we tend to blame their personality ("He's rude"), but when we behave badly, we blame the situation ("I was tired"). Culture also plays a role. In some cultures, direct eye contact signals honesty; in others, it can come across as disrespectful. What seems confident in one country may seem arrogant in another. None of this means we should ignore our instincts completely. But it does suggest that we should hold our first impressions lightly, look for evidence, and give people the same benefit of the doubt that we would want them to give us.

questions.q: Which candidate would most people instinctively prefer, and why is that a problem?
questions.answer: The confident one, although nothing shows who would do the job better.

questions.q: What is the fundamental attribution error?
questions.answer: Blaming others' personality for their bad behavior but blaming the situation for our own.

questions.q: How can eye contact be interpreted differently?
questions.answer: In some cultures it signals honesty; in others it can seem disrespectful.

questions.q: What does the writer recommend?
questions.answer: Hold first impressions lightly, look for evidence and give people the benefit of the doubt.

writing.model:
My Aunt Zélia

At first glance, my Aunt Zélia comes across as a rather serious woman. She's tall, wears her grey hair in a tight bun and tends to look at people over the top of her glasses, as if she were assessing them. Strangers often find her intimidating.

But anyone who spends more than ten minutes with her soon discovers that she's one of the most down-to-earth and generous people you could meet. She'll stop to talk to the man who sells popcorn on her street, and she'll remember the names of all his children. When I was a teenager, she would call me every Sunday just to ask about my week, and she never once judged me, even when I made terrible decisions.

She isn't perfect, of course. She's incredibly stubborn: once she's made up her mind, there's no point arguing. And she WILL insist on giving you a second plate of food, no matter how many times you say you're full. She's forever telling me I look thin!

Still, I can't imagine my life without her. If I've learned anything from Aunt Zélia, it's that the people who seem the toughest on the outside are often the softest inside.

culture_note.title: Diretos x indiretos
culture_note.text_pt: O que é "confiante" ou "educado" muda entre culturas. Nos EUA, autopromoção e contato visual forte costumam ser vistos como confiança; no Japão, modéstia é valorizada; no Reino Unido, o **understatement** (dizer menos do que se sente) é comum: "It's not bad" pode significar "é ótimo!". No B2, perceber essas nuances é parte da fluência.

summary_pt: will / would = hábito característico (would: só ações).

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs: tipos e posição do objeto
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Intransitivos (sem objeto):** fall out, make up, break up, drift apart, grow up
"We **fell out** last year, but we've **made up** now."

**2. Separáveis (transitivos)** — o objeto pode ficar **no meio ou no fim**; mas se for **pronome**, **tem que ficar no meio**:
- "She **let her friends down**." / "She **let down her friends**." ✅
- "She **let them down**." ✅ / ❌ "She let down them."
- Outros: bring up (criar), turn down (recusar), cheer up (animar), talk into (convencer), ask out (convidar para sair)

**3. Inseparáveis** — o objeto vem sempre **depois** da partícula:
- "I can always **count on her**." (❌ count her on) / "She **takes after her mother**." (puxou à mãe) / "I **ran into** an old friend." (encontrei por acaso)

**4. Três partes** (verbo + advérbio + preposição) — sempre inseparáveis:
- **put up with** (tolerar), **look up to** (admirar), **look down on** (menosprezar), **get on with** (dar-se bem), **catch up with** (colocar o papo em dia), **come up with** (ter uma ideia), **stand up for** (defender), **fall out with** (brigar com)
- "I **look up to** my grandmother." / "How do you **put up with** the noise?"

💡 **Dica de registro:** phrasal verbs são mais **informais**; em textos formais, muitas vezes existe um verbo latino equivalente: put up with → **tolerate**; fall out → **argue**; look up to → **admire**; bring up → **raise**.

rows: She brought up three kids. / She brought three kids up.

examples.en: We used to be inseparable, but we drifted apart when she moved abroad.

grammar.tip_pt: Aprenda phrasal verbs **em contexto e por tema** (relacionamentos, trabalho, viagens), nunca em listas alfabéticas. E use um bom dicionário (Cambridge, Oxford Learner's) para saber se são separáveis.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Com pronome, o objeto vai no meio do phrasal verb separável.

common_mistakes.wrong: I can't put up this noise.
common_mistakes.right: I can't put up with this noise.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Put up with tem três partes.

common_mistakes.wrong: We made up with each other after we fell out with.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Sem objeto, use as formas intransitivas (fall out, make up).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em phrasal verbs, a **partícula** costuma ser a sílaba mais forte: "We fell **OUT**", "They broke **UP**", "Don't let me **DOWN**". Em verbos de três partes, a força fica no meio: "put **UP** with", "look **UP** to".

lines.en: Do you still see Carol? You two used to be inseparable.

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: Not really. We drifted apart after she moved to Recife. And then we fell out over something silly.

lines.speaker: Lia

lines.speaker: Jade

lines.speaker: Lia

lines.speaker: Lia

lines.speaker: Jade

listening.title: Radio: what makes friendships last?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre amizades na vida adulta.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: One of the most common things people tell us is that they've drifted apart from friends without any real conflict. Life just gets in the way: people move, have children, change jobs. Research suggests that adult friendships need regular contact to survive — not necessarily long conversations, but small gestures, like sending a message or catching up over coffee. Another key factor is how people deal with conflict. Friends who fall out but then talk openly and make up often end up closer than before. On the other hand, friendships where people keep putting up with things they don't like, without saying anything, tend to fade. So my advice is simple: reach out, and if something bothers you, bring it up — kindly.

questions.q: Why do many adults drift apart from friends?
questions.answer: Life gets in the way: moving, having children, changing jobs.

questions.q: What do adult friendships need to survive?
questions.answer: Regular contact — small gestures like messages or coffee.

questions.q: What happens to friends who fall out and then make up openly?
questions.answer: They often end up closer than before.

questions.q: What's the researcher's advice?
questions.answer: Reach out, and if something bothers you, bring it up kindly.

reading.title: The friendship recession
reading.text: In recent years, several surveys in the United States and other countries have suggested that adults have fewer close friends than they used to. Some commentators have even started talking about a "friendship recession". The reasons are complex. People work longer hours, move more often for jobs and spend more time online. Many say they simply don't have time to catch up with friends, and that friendships slowly fade without anyone falling out. Researchers also point out that making new friends as an adult is harder than at school or university, where we meet the same people every day without trying. One frequently quoted study by Jeffrey Hall estimated that it takes around 50 hours of time together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. That's a lot of coffees. However, there are reasons for optimism. Many people are deliberately making time for friendship: joining running clubs, book clubs and volunteer groups, where repeated contact happens naturally. As one participant put it, "I used to wait for friendships to happen. Now I put the effort in — and I've never felt less lonely."

questions.q: What is the "friendship recession"?
questions.answer: The idea that adults have fewer close friends than they used to.

questions.q: Why is making friends harder as an adult?
questions.answer: We don't meet the same people every day without trying, as at school or university.

questions.q: How many hours does it take to become close friends, according to the study?
questions.answer: More than 200 hours.

questions.q: What are some people doing about it?
questions.answer: Joining clubs and groups where repeated contact happens naturally.

Hi Carol,

I know it's been ages since we last spoke, and I'm really sorry I haven't been in touch. After the wedding, life just got in the way — new job, new apartment, and suddenly two years had gone by. I've thought about you so many times.

The other day I ran into your mum at the bakery near my old house. She told me you'd been going through a really tough time around the time of my wedding. I had no idea, and I feel awful that I didn't reach out. I think I was hurt that you couldn't come, and instead of bringing it up, I just stayed quiet. That wasn't fair to either of us.

Anyway, I'd love to catch up properly. I've got loads of news (yes, I finally gave up my terrible job at the bank!), and I want to hear everything about your life in Recife. I'm actually going to be there for a conference next month. Could we meet up for lunch?

Lots of love,
Jade

grammar.title: Advanced comparisons
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Modificar comparativos** (o quanto maior/menor):
- grande diferença: **much / far / a lot / considerably / significantly** + comparativo → "Rent is **far higher** than it was in 2010."
- pequena diferença: **slightly / a bit / a little / marginally** → "Gen Z is **slightly more** likely to..."
- também com superlativos: "**by far the** biggest change" / "**easily the** best"

**2. As... as (com modificadores):**
- **just as** (exatamente tão): "Young people are **just as** hard-working **as** their parents."
- **not quite as / not nearly as / nowhere near as** (não tão / nem de longe tão): "Buying a house is **nowhere near as** easy **as** it was."
- **twice / three times as... as** (o dobro / o triplo): "Houses cost **three times as much as** they did."
- **the same as / similar to / different from**

**3. Comparativos duplos (mudança progressiva / correlação):**
- **-er and -er / more and more** (cada vez mais): "Life is getting **more and more** expensive." / "Phones are getting **smaller and smaller**."
- **The + comparativo..., the + comparativo** (quanto mais..., mais...): "**The more** you read, **the better** you write." / "**The older** I get, **the less** I care about what people think." / "**The sooner, the better.**"

**4. Linguagem para evitar estereótipos:** use **tend to**, **on average**, **many / some (but not all)**, **compared with**: "**On average**, Gen Z **tends to** change jobs more often **than** previous generations."

rows: We're just as worried as they were.
It's nowhere near as cheap as before.
The more I learn, the less I know.

examples.en: On average, young people today are far more likely to rent than to own a home.

examples.pt: Quanto mais tempo passo com minha avó, mais percebo o quanto ela passou.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português dizemos "**cada vez mais caro**"; em inglês, **more and more expensive** ou, para adjetivos curtos, **cheaper and cheaper**. Nunca "each time more" ❌.

common_mistakes.right: It's getting more and more difficult.
common_mistakes.why_pt: "Cada vez mais" = more and more / -er and -er.

common_mistakes.wrong: More you study, more you learn.

common_mistakes.why_pt: A estrutura exige the nas duas partes.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Nas frases "the more..., the more...", há duas partes com ritmo paralelo e uma pausa no meio: "The **MORE** you **READ** ↗ | the **BET**ter you **WRITE** ↘." A voz sobe na primeira parte e desce na segunda.

listening.title: Generations at work
listening.context_pt: Uma consultora de RH fala sobre equipes com várias gerações.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Today, many workplaces have four or even five generations working side by side. Managers often ask me whether younger employees are really that different. My answer: slightly, but nowhere near as much as the headlines suggest. Surveys show that, on average, younger workers tend to value flexibility and feedback a bit more, while older workers tend to value stability. But when you look at what people want most — fair pay, respect and meaningful work — the generations are remarkably similar. The bigger problem is stereotypes. The more we assume that a 60-year-old can't learn new technology, or that a 25-year-old won't stay in a job, the worse our teams work. The best approach is mentoring in both directions: older employees share experience, younger ones share new tools. The more they learn from each other, the better.

questions.answer: Slightly, but nowhere near as much as headlines suggest.

reading.title: Are young people really so different?
reading.text: Every generation seems to believe that the next one is lazier, more selfish and more addicted to whatever technology is new. Similar complaints about young people can be found in texts from centuries ago. Today, the target is often Generation Z, described in headlines as anxious, glued to their phones and unwilling to work hard. But how much of this is true? The data paint a more complex picture. On the one hand, young people today do spend considerably more time online than previous generations did at the same age, and surveys in several countries suggest that reported levels of anxiety among teenagers have risen. On the other hand, many members of Gen Z drink far less alcohol and smoke much less than their parents did as teenagers, and they're often just as interested in meaningful work. Economic conditions matter too. In many countries, housing has become far more expensive relative to income, making it nowhere near as easy for young people to reach traditional milestones like buying a home. Researchers increasingly argue that differences between generations are often less about character and more about circumstances. Put simply: the more you change the world young people grow up in, the more their choices will change too.

questions.answer: That it's lazier, more selfish and more addicted to new technology.

questions.q: In what ways might they be "better" than their parents at the same age?

questions.q: What do researchers increasingly argue?
questions.answer: Differences are less about character and more about circumstances.

writing.task: Write a comparison essay (200–250 words): "Young people today have a better life than their grandparents did." Discuss both sides and give your opinion. Use advanced comparatives and careful generalizations.

writing.model:
It is often said that young people today have a far better life than their grandparents did. While there is some truth in this, the picture is much more complex.

On the one hand, in many ways life has become considerably easier. Most young people today have access to far more information, healthcare and opportunities than their grandparents could have imagined. In Brazil, for example, the average life expectancy is significantly higher than it was in the 1960s, and many more people go to university. Technology also allows us to stay in touch with friends and family who live thousands of kilometers away.

On the other hand, some aspects of life have become harder and harder. Housing is nowhere near as affordable as it was, and stable, lifelong jobs are much less common. Many young people also report higher levels of anxiety, partly because of the constant pressure of social media.

In my opinion, it is misleading to say that one generation has it better than another. Each generation faces different challenges. My grandparents had fewer choices, but they had more stability; we have more freedom, but less security. Rather than competing over who suffered more, I believe that the more generations listen to each other, the better we will understand the world we share.

grammar.title: Hedging and softening
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Hedging** é suavizar uma afirmação para soar menos absoluto, mais educado ou mais preciso. É essencial em reuniões, textos acadêmicos e conversas delicadas.

**1. Verbos que suavizam:** **seem / appear / tend / suggest / indicate**
- "The plan **seems to** have some problems." (em vez de "The plan has problems")
- "The data **suggest** that..." / "It **appears that** prices will rise."

**2. Modais de possibilidade:** **might / may / could / would**
- "That **might** not be the best approach." / "I **would** say that..." / "I **would have thought**..."

**3. Advérbios e expressões de grau:** **perhaps, possibly, arguably, presumably, to some extent, in some ways, relatively, fairly, rather, a little, somewhat**
- "It's **arguably** the most important issue." / "I **somewhat** disagree."

**4. Estruturas impessoais:** **It could be argued that... / It is often said that... / There is some evidence that...**

**5. Discordância suave** (nunca "You're wrong"):
- "**I'm not sure I agree.**" / "**I see what you mean, but**..." / "**I'm not entirely convinced.**"
- "**Couldn't it also be argued that**...?" (pergunta negativa = sugestão educada)
- "**With respect**, I see it a bit differently."

**6. Quantificadores cuidadosos:** many (not all), some, most, a significant number of — em vez de **all / everyone / never / always**.

⚠️ Não exagere: hedging demais soa inseguro. Use mais em **opiniões e temas sensíveis**, menos em **fatos claros**.

rows: I'm not entirely sure that idea would work.
This is arguably the best solution.
There seems to be a serious problem with corruption in some areas.
I think we might be seeing this from different angles.

listening.title: Academic hedging
listening.context_pt: Uma professora universitária explica por que a linguagem acadêmica é cheia de "talvez".

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: Students often ask me why academic writing is so full of words like "may", "suggest" and "appear". Isn't it better to be confident? The answer is that good researchers try not to claim more than their evidence shows. If one study finds that coffee drinkers live longer, a careful scientist won't write "Coffee makes you live longer." They'll write something like "The results suggest that moderate coffee consumption may be associated with a lower risk of mortality." It's less exciting, but it's more honest. The study can't prove that coffee is the cause — perhaps coffee drinkers also tend to have other healthy habits. Hedging isn't weakness. It's precision. And in a world full of exaggerated headlines, I'd argue we need much more of it.

questions.q: Why is academic writing full of words like "may" and "suggest"?
questions.answer: Researchers try not to claim more than their evidence shows.

questions.q: Why can't the study prove that coffee is the cause?

questions.q: What does the professor say hedging is?
questions.answer: Not weakness, but precision.

reading.title: How to disagree well
reading.text: In 2008, computer scientist and essayist Paul Graham proposed a "hierarchy of disagreement" — a pyramid showing different ways people argue, from the least to the most useful. At the bottom is name-calling: attacking the person rather than the idea ("You're an idiot"). Slightly higher is responding to tone ("Why are you being so aggressive?"), which avoids the actual argument. In the middle is contradiction: simply stating the opposite view without evidence. Near the top is counterargument — giving reasons and evidence for a different position — and at the very top is refutation: identifying exactly where the other person's argument goes wrong and explaining why. Graham's model has been widely shared online, perhaps because many public debates seem to be stuck at the bottom of the pyramid. Social media, which rewards quick and emotional reactions, arguably makes things worse. Psychologists who study conflict suggest a few habits that may help: listen to understand rather than to reply, summarize the other person's view before responding ("So you're saying..."), and look for common ground. Disagreeing well doesn't mean avoiding conflict. It means making conflict productive.

questions.q: What is at the bottom of the hierarchy of disagreement?
questions.answer: Name-calling (attacking the person, not the idea).

questions.q: What is the difference between contradiction and counterargument?
questions.answer: Contradiction states the opposite without evidence; counterargument gives reasons and evidence.

questions.q: Why might social media make things worse?
questions.answer: It rewards quick and emotional reactions.

questions.q: Name two habits that may help.
questions.answer: Listen to understand, summarize the other person's view, look for common ground.

speaking.instruction: "Diplomatic debate": discuss two sensitive topics (e.g., "Should social media be banned for under-16s?", "Should the working week be four days?"). Rule: you must use at least 3 hedging expressions per turn and summarize the other person's view before responding.
speaking.instruction_pt: "Debate diplomático": discutam dois temas sensíveis (ex.: "As redes sociais deveriam ser proibidas para menores de 16?", "A semana de trabalho deveria ter quatro dias?"). Regra: use pelo menos 3 expressões de hedging por turno e resuma a opinião do outro antes de responder.

Are Brazilians generally more direct or indirect than other cultures you know?
Where are you on Graham's pyramid of disagreement when you argue online?
How do you react when someone disagrees with you strongly?
When is it better to agree to disagree?

writing.task: Write a reply (180–220 words) to a colleague's email proposing a change you partly disagree with (e.g., moving the team back to the office five days a week). Acknowledge their points, disagree diplomatically and suggest common ground.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma resposta (180–220 palavras) ao e-mail de um colega propondo uma mudança com a qual você discorda em parte (ex.: voltar ao escritório cinco dias por semana). Reconheça os pontos dele, discorde com diplomacia e sugira um meio-termo.
writing.model:
Hi Mark,

Thank you for sharing your proposal about returning to the office five days a week. I can see you've put a lot of thought into it, and I agree with several of your points. It's true that new team members seem to learn faster when they can sit with more experienced colleagues, and some of our brainstorming sessions have arguably been less creative online.

That said, I'm not entirely convinced that a full return is the best solution for everyone. Our productivity data from the last year appear to show that focused tasks, such as writing reports and analyzing data, have actually improved since we became hybrid. In addition, several team members have long commutes, and a sudden change might affect morale and, potentially, retention.

Perhaps there's some common ground here. Would it be worth trying a model with three fixed office days for collaboration and training, and two flexible days for focused work? We could review the results after three months and adjust if necessary.

I'd be happy to discuss this further in our next meeting. I really appreciate you opening the conversation.

Best regards,
Luana

culture_note.title: Assuntos que muitos evitam no trabalho
culture_note.text_pt: Em muitos ambientes profissionais anglófonos, há um consenso informal de evitar **politics, religion and money** (política, religião e dinheiro) com pessoas que você não conhece bem — especialmente salários. Mas isso está mudando: em alguns países, a transparência salarial (**pay transparency**) virou até lei.
